topic.title: Translating your documentation with Content Fusion

body.p: Leveraging AI, Content Fusion can translate your documentation automatically. But even with AI, no translation can be right without context: your product’s terminology and the terms your team has settled on. What follows is a journal of translating our own user guide, and what we found when we reviewed the result.

section.title: Step 1: Running a translation
section.p: In the project workspace, open Translation Jobs, choose New translation, pick the publications and the target languages, and start the job. Both are multi-select, so one job can produce several translations.

An AI agent then walks the DITA map, translates the topics, and writes a parallel language folder per target. The job's Bring into Workspace action brings the translations into the workspace, where they are ordinary files to review and commit. A publication for the new language is added to ditaProject.xml automatically, and the translated publication shows up in the Context publication drop-down.
The run also leaves a translation-index.xml file in the workspace. It is part of the translation state, so commit it along with the translated files.
The New translation dialog points at a .contentfusion/i18n/agent-instructions.md, a file in the workspace that the agent reads before it starts, and creates it automatically.

section.title: Step 2: Review — not quite right
section.p: We translated four topics of our guide into French with the instructions field left empty. We then pointed Claude Code (Opus 5) at the translated files together with the English source and our own UI resource bundle, and asked what was wrong. Its summary: The French is fluent and grammatical. But it is not correctly localized.

li.p: Terminology that contradicted our own product. Content Fusion ships a French UI, in a resource bundle the translation agent never saw. So the guide told French users about validations entrantes where the product says Commits entrants, and called their role Réviseur where the product label is Examinateur:
li.codeblock:
"Incoming commits" — the product says Commits entrants fr-FR/DITA-cf/topics/cf-projects-workspace.dita:6,22,28 EN ...review incoming commits, and commit your changes. -FR consulter les validations entrantes et de valider vos modifications. +FR consulter les commits entrants et de valider vos modifications. "Reviewer" role — the product label is Examinateur fr-FR/DITA-cf/topics/review-tasks-intro.dita:47 (+ réviseur(s) at :6, :19, :52) EN
  • Reviewer - Reviews the content, adds comments... -FR
  • Réviseur - Examine le contenu, ajoute des commentaires... +FR
  • Examinateur - Examine le contenu, ajoute des commentaires...

ul.li: One term, several renderings. dépôt six times in cf-projects.dita, référentiel twice in cf-projects-workspace.dita, and never mixed inside a single file. Every file was internally consistent and disagreed with its neighbour. The same English phrase Author platform user role came out as three different French phrases across three files.

No French typography. French puts a non-breaking space before : ; ! ?. The fr-FR/ tree contained not a single U+00A0 or U+202F across the 11 places that needed one, and with a plain space the renderer can orphan the colon onto the next line.

Emphasis drift. The English consistently bolds only the role name; the French moved the <b> boundary, and in opposite directions in different files — swallowing the whole phrase in cf-projects.dita and review-tasks-intro.dita, correct in types_of_review_tasks.dita. Elsewhere the article got pulled inside the bold, so the emphasized string was no longer the product term.

Grammar errors, which we had not expected: a missing plural agreement in an <indexterm> (Tâches de révision indépendante), right in one file and wrong in its parallel one; and a role name mistranslated into the subject-matter-expert platform.

Non-native phrasing. The prose was grammatically correct and still read like a translation — literal where a native speaker would have reached for the ordinary word. bande is a strip of material, while a strip in a UI is a bandeau; certains membres sélectionnés is a pleonasm; prendre en charge was used for an abstract subject, where a review task does not handle a workflow but is part of one.

section.p: A human reviewer then went through the AI's list, and did not accept all of it — the emphasis-drift findings in particular were judged not to matter much in the rendered output. The terminology mismatches were the important find, because they generalize past our product: the AI can write beautiful French and still be wrong about your software. The words on your screens are a fact, not an inference.
The same pattern showed up in Romanian, translated from the same guide: correct grammar, English syntax carried over.
section.codeblock:
EN As a cloud service, Oxygen Content Fusion separates collaboration workspaces into Organizations. RO Ca serviciu bazat pe cloud, Oxygen Content Fusion separă spațiile de lucru pentru colaborare în Organizații. RO (localized) Fiind un serviciu cloud, Oxygen Content Fusion organizează spațiile de colaborare în organizații.
EN Review Task Roles RO Roluri pentru sarcina de revizuire <- generic singular translated literally RO (correct) Roluri pentru sarcini de revizuire

section.title: Step 3: Fine-tuning
section.p: Every pass re-translates every file and translation costs tokens, so we developed against four topics rather than the real guide. That small sample was enough to reveal systematic defects without spending tokens on the full guide, but a larger run could reveal additional issues and establish how widespread each problem is.
Two rules earned their place in agent-instructions.md. One worked, and the one that did not turned out to be the more instructive of the two.

section.title: A glossary of the application's UI strings
section.p: The terminology findings are not something to hope the model infers. The shipped UI strings have to be handed to the agent as data, because the agent is sandboxed to our DITA workspace and cannot reach into our application's repository. So we put a ui-glossary-fr-FR.md file in the .contentfusion/i18n/ directory, holding the shipped English→French strings from our own application.
section.codeblock:
## Not translated by the product — shown in English - `DITA Map` (key `ditamap`) - `Org-level role` (key `organization.role`)
## Labels - `Add reviewer` -> `Ajouter un examinateur` - `Incoming commits` -> `Commits entrants` - `Repository` -> `Dépôt` - `Workspace` -> `Espace de travail`
section.p: That first list earns its place as much as the pairs do. Where the running French UI shows English for a label, the manual has to as well — and you only know which labels those are by looking them up per language.
Then point agent-instructions.md at it. Relative links are resolved automatically, so naming the file is enough:
section.codeblock: ### Terminology — the shipped UI is the authority .contentfusion/i18n/ui-glossary-fr-FR.md holds the product's shipped en→fr UI strings. Read it before translating. Any text inside `<uicontrol>` or `<menucascade>`, and every button, field, view, page, and role name, must reuse the shipped French string verbatim. Never invent a French label that contradicts a shipped one. If a label is absent from the glossary, translate it once and reuse that exact rendering everywhere.
section.p: For the terms the glossary cannot answer — the concepts your documentation presents that have no UI label — decide the answer yourself instead of asking every worker to arrive at the same one, and name the plausible-but-wrong rendering explicitly. The negatives are what stop it, and every one of these is a defect we actually saw:
section.codeblock: - repository → le dépôt — never référentiel - reviewer → l'examinateur — never réviseur - incoming commits → les commits entrants — never validations entrantes - DITA Map → DITA Map (the French UI leaves it in English)
section.p: Extracting that list is itself a job you can delegate: ask an agent to walk the content for the terms it uses, both the ones carrying DITA markup (<uicontrol>, <term>) and the unmarked concepts the application presents, then filter by hand and fill in the approved target-language rendering. Two side effects are worth having: a term the extraction cannot place is usually a concept your documentation is missing, and an agent that does not know the right rendering for a term should be told to say so rather than invent one.

section.title: A rule that was understood and still did not land
section.p: The other rule we added to agent-instructions.md was the typography one, because the baseline had none of it:
section.codeblock: ### French typography Use a non-breaking space (U+00A0) before `:` `;` `!` `?` and inside `« »`. Never a plain space.
section.p: It did not work, and the way it failed is the most useful thing we learned. The agent reported back:
section.codeblock:
I was unable to reliably insert a genuine non-breaking space (U+00A0) before `:` through the available editing tools in this session — several attempts to inject the character were silently normalized to a regular space by the tool layer. [...] I used a normal space before colons in both files instead of the requested nbsp.
[main agent] Four clusters completed. One sub-agent (review-tasks cluster) flagged that it couldn't reliably insert U+00A0 non-breaking spaces and fell back to regular spaces before colons — a project-instruction compliance gap.
section.p: So an instruction can be understood, attempted, and still not land, because the model cannot reliably emit the character you asked for. The instruction to write instead is the XML character entity —   — which is plain ASCII and survives the tool layer.

ol.li: Terminology is data, not inference. The AI can write fluent, grammatical prose in the target language and still contradict every button in your product. The shipped UI strings are the authority, and the agent cannot see them — you have to bring them into the workspace as a glossary.

Consistency across files does not come for free. Each file was internally consistent and disagreed with its neighbour, which is what parallel per-file translation produces: every worker inventing its own private dialect. Freeze the terms yourself, and name the wrong rendering as well as the right one.

Look up each language separately. Which labels your product translates, which it leaves in English, and what the accepted rendering is for a technical term — none of that transfers from one locale to the next.

An instruction can be understood and still not land. The non-breaking space was requested, attempted, reported as impossible, and silently normalized away. Prefer instructions the tooling cannot corrupt — an ASCII character entity over an exotic codepoint — and verify the output rather than trusting that a rule was applied.

Grammatically correct is not localized. The literal translations, carried English syntax and calques are what a reader notices first and what no grammar check flags. Asking for natural French sets the register but fixes no individual slip; a style-notes section that names the slips you have seen (bande is a strip of material, a UI strip is a bandeau) changes the output.

Review with AI first, then with a person. The AI review found the terminology, typography and markup problems quickly, across the whole tree, with file and line references. The human pass is what decided which of them mattered — some findings were downgraded on the second look. Neither pass replaces the other, and a review step is worth building into the translation job itself.

Develop against a small sample. Four topics were enough to expose defects that are systematic by nature, at a fraction of the token cost of the full guide. Only the scale of each problem needs the real publication.
Write down observed mistakes, not general advice. Every line in our instructions file exists because a specific defect happened. Start the style-notes section empty and add to it after each run.
